newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania main oil trader says still handling import.
newsitem.headline: Romania main oil trader says still handling import.

text.p: Romania's main oil trader Petrolexportimport SA bitterly rejected on Friday allegations that it no longer handled crude imports following a police investigation.
"Such allegations are nonsensical. Petrolexportimport functions normally," company deputy general manager Valeriu Iancu told Reuters.
His remarks were in response to reports carried by oil market newsletters this week that the company had been bypassed, with crude imports now handled by the office of Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea.
"This is ridiculous. We are fully in charge of our operations," Iancu said.

The stories came after local press reports last Friday that police had launched investigations into alleged corruption involving Petrolexportimport general manager Aurel Bacila and several local oil companies.
Bacila denied the accusations in a state television interview the same day.

"It is true that the police is investigating allegations that Petrolexportimport has favoured local private oil firms by helping them to get better export deals. It is normal for them to check," Iancu said.
Operators at the main oil terminal in the Black Sea port of Constanta confirmed that Petrolexportimport's imports and exports were carried out directly by the company.

"Petrolexportimport has now the Saphire loading some 60,000 tonnes of petrol for export. The Sea Dancer will arrive by February 1 to discharge 112,000 tonnes of crude consigned to Petrolexport," an operator said by telephone from Constanta.
Iancu said a signing ceremony for $200 of revolving credit arranged by Chase Manhattan Corp for Petrolexportimport would take place in London on February 3 "as was scheduled".
The syndicated loan will help Romania carry out smoothly its import programme of some 800,000 tonnes of crude a month.
"Being a revolving credit we talk in fact about some $600 million till the end of the year, which we will spend on part of our crude imports," Iancu said.
Romania needs to import large quantities of crude oil for domestic demand and to keep in operation its oversized refining capacity inherited from the former communist regime.
